subject: history
topic: The Stanford prison experiment was not what you were taught
angle: Archival evidence shows that the guards' behavior was not a spontaneous result of their roles but was directly encouraged and instructed by the experimenters.
title: The coached reality of SPE

reveal.headline: The guards were told how to act.
reveal.body: Experimenters gave the guards precise instructions on how to treat the prisoners and encouraged them to adopt tough roles.

explain.headline: It was not a spontaneous behavior.
explain.body: The study drew on a prison experiment conducted by students three months earlier. The behavior was a result of coaching and prior work.

matters.headline: The power was manufactured.
matters.body: That may be why the results look like a study on human nature when they might actually be a study on how people follow orders.

example.headline: A supervisor giving a direct order.
example.body: You stand in a hallway and watch someone tell you exactly how to behave in your job. You do it because they told you to.

verdict: The evidence indicates that the Stanford Prison Experiment was heavily influenced by external instructions and prior student work rather than being a purely organic demonstration of role conformity.
caveat: While the sources highlight significant flaws and coaching, they also note that the interpersonal power dynamics in the simulation successfully mimicked those of a real prison.
caption:
The Stanford Prison Experiment is often cited as proof of inherent human cruelty.

Evidence shows the guards were directly coached by experimenters and the study relied on a student project from three months prior. While the simulation successfully mimicked real prison power dynamics, the behavior was not purely organic.

Do you follow instructions because you believe in them or because you were told to?
